{{Short description|Type of mathematical group}}
'''Arithmetic Fuchsian groups''' are a special class of [[Fuchsian group]]s constructed using [[Order (ring theory)|order]]s in [[quaternion algebra]]s. They are particular instances of [[arithmetic group]]s. The prototypical example of an arithmetic Fuchsian group is the [[modular group]] <math> \mathrm{PSL}_2(\Z )</math>. They, and the [[hyperbolic manifold|hyperbolic surface]] associated to their action on the [[hyperbolic plane]], often exhibit particularly regular behaviour among Fuchsian groups and hyperbolic surfaces.

== Definition and examples ==

=== Quaternion algebras ===
{{Main article| Quaternion algebra}}

A quaternion algebra over a field <math>F</math> is a four-dimensional [[Central simple algebra|central simple]] <math>F</math>-algebra. A quaternion algebra has a basis <math>1, i, j, ij</math>, where <math>i^2, j^2 \in F^\times</math> and <math>ij = -ji</math>.

A quaternion algebra is said to be split over <math>F</math> if it is isomorphic as an <math>F</math>-algebra to the algebra of matrices <math>M_2(F)</math>.

If <math>\sigma</math> is an embedding of <math>F</math> into a field <math>E</math>, then we denote by <math>A \otimes_\sigma E</math> the algebra obtained by [[Extension of scalars|extending scalars]] from <math>F</math> to <math>E</math>, where we view <math>F</math> as a subfield of <math>E</math> via <math>\sigma</math>.

=== Arithmetic Fuchsian groups ===

A subgroup of <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\R)</math> is said to be ''derived from a quaternion algebra'' if it can be obtained through the following construction. Let <math>F</math> be a [[totally real number field]] and <math>A</math> a quaternion algebra over <math>F</math> satisfying the following conditions. First there is a unique embedding <math>\sigma: F \hookrightarrow \R</math> such that <math>A \otimes_\sigma \R</math> is split over <math>\R</math>; we denote by <math>\phi : A \otimes_\sigma \R \to M_2(\R)</math> an isomorphism of <math>\R</math>-algebras. We also ask that for all other embeddings <math>\tau</math> the algebra <math>A \otimes_\tau \R</math> is not split (this is equivalent to its being isomorphic to the [[Hamilton quaternions]]). Next we need an order <math>\mathcal O</math> in <math>A</math>. Let <math>\mathcal O^1</math> be the group of elements in <math>\mathcal O</math> of reduced norm 1 and let <math>\Gamma</math> be its image in <math>M_2(\R )</math> via <math>\phi</math>. Then the image of <math>\Gamma</math> is a subgroup of <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\R )</math> (since the reduced norm of a matrix algebra is just the determinant) and we can consider the Fuchsian group which is its image in <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\R)</math>.

The main fact about these groups is that they are discrete subgroups and they have finite covolume for the [[Haar measure]] on <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\R).</math> Moreover, the construction above yields a cocompact subgroup [[if and only if]] the algebra <math>A</math> is not split over <math>F</math>. The discreteness is a rather immediate consequence of the fact that <math>A</math> is only split at one real embedding. The finiteness of covolume is harder to prove.{{sfn|Katok|1992}}

An ''arithmetic Fuchsian group'' is any subgroup of <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\R)</math> which is [[commensurability (group theory)|commensurable]] to a group derived from a quaternion algebra. It follows immediately from this definition that arithmetic Fuchsian groups are discrete and of finite covolume (this means that they are [[Lattice (discrete subgroup)|lattices]] in <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\R)</math>).

=== Examples ===

The simplest example of an arithmetic Fuchsian group is the modular <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\Z),</math> which is obtained by the construction above with <math>A = M_2(\Q)</math> and <math>\mathcal O = M_2(\Z).</math> By taking [[Eichler order]]s in <math>A</math> we obtain subgroups <math>\Gamma_0(N)</math> for <math>N \geqslant 2</math> of finite index in <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\Z)</math> which can be explicitly written as follows:

:<math> \Gamma_0(N) = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \in \mathrm{PSL}_2(\Z) :  c = 0 \pmod N \right\}.</math>

The arithmeticity of such subgroups follows from the fact that they have finite-index in the arithmetic group <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\Z )</math>; they belong to a more general class of finite-index subgroups, namely [[Congruence subgroup|congruence subgroups]].

Any order in a quaternion algebra over <math>\Q</math> which is not split over <math>\Q</math> but splits over <math>\R</math> yields a cocompact arithmetic Fuchsian group. There is a plentiful supply of such algebras.{{sfn|Katok|1992|loc=section 5.6}}

More generally, all orders in quaternion algebras (satisfying the above conditions) which are not <math>M_2(\Q)</math> yield cocompact subgroups. A further example of particular interest is obtained by taking <math>A</math> to be the [[Hurwitz quaternion]]s.

=== Maximal subgroups ===

A natural question is to identify those among arithmetic Fuchsian groups which are not strictly contained in a larger discrete subgroup. These are called ''maximal'' Kleinian groups, and it is possible to give a complete classification in a given arithmetic commensurability class. A theorem of [[Grigory Margulis|Margulis]] implies that a lattice in <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\Complex)</math> is arithmetic if and only if it is commensurable to infinitely many maximal Kleinian groups.

=== Congruence subgroups ===

A ''principal congruence subgroup'' of <math>\Gamma = \mathrm{SL}_2(\Z)</math> is a subgroup of the form

:<math> \Gamma(N) =  \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \in \mathrm{PSL}_2(\Z) : a,d = 1 \pmod N, \, b,c = 0 \pmod N  \right\}</math>

for some <math>N \geqslant 1.</math> These are finite-index normal subgroups, and the quotient <math>\Gamma/\Gamma(N)</math> is isomorphic to the finite group <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\Z /N\Z).</math> A ''congruence subgroup'' of <math>\Gamma</math> is by definition a subgroup which contains a principal [[congruence subgroup]] (these are the groups which are defined by taking the matrices in <math>\Gamma</math> which satisfy certain congruences modulo an integer, hence the name).

Notably, not all finite-index subgroups of <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\Z)</math> are congruence subgroups. A nice way to see this is to observe that <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\Z)</math> has subgroups which surject onto the [[alternating group]] <math>A_n</math> for arbitrary <math>n,</math> and since for large <math>n</math> the group <math>A_n</math> is not a subgroup of <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\Z/N \Z)</math> for any <math>N</math>, these subgroups cannot be congruence subgroups. In fact there are many more non-congruence than congruence subgroups in <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\Z)</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lubotzky |first1=Alexander |last2=Segal |first2=Dan  |date=2003 |title=Subgroup growth |chapter= Chapter 7 |publisher=Birkhäuser}}</ref>

The notion of a congruence subgroup generalizes to cocompact arithmetic Fuchsian groups, and the results above also hold in this general setting.

=== Construction via quadratic forms ===

There is an isomorphism between <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\R)</math> and the connected component of the [[orthogonal group]] <math>\mathrm{SO}(2,1)</math> given by the action of the former by conjugation on the space of matrices of [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]] zero, on which the determinant induces the structure of a real [[quadratic space]] of signature (2,1). Arithmetic Fuchsian groups can be constructed directly in the latter group by taking the integral points in the orthogonal group associated to [[Quadratic form|quadratic forms]] defined over [[number fields]] (and satisfying certain conditions).

In this correspondence, the modular group is associated up to commensurability to the group <math>\mathrm{SO}(2,1)(\Z).</math><ref>{{cite web |url=https://lamington.wordpress.com/2014/05/17/a-tale-of-two-arithmetic-lattices/ |title=A tale of two arithmetic lattices |last=Calegari |first=Danny | date=May 17, 2014 |access-date=20 June 2016}}</ref>

=== Arithmetic Kleinian groups ===
{{Main article | Arithmetic hyperbolic 3-manifold}}

The construction above can be adapted to obtain subgroups in <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\Complex)</math>: instead of asking for <math>F</math> to be totally real and <math>A</math> to be split at exactly one real embedding, one asks for <math>F</math> to have exactly one complex embedding up to complex conjugacy, at which <math>A</math> is automatically split, and that <math>A</math> is not split at any embedding <math>F \hookrightarrow \R</math>. The subgroups of <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\Complex)</math> commensurable to those obtained by this construction are called ''arithmetic Kleinian groups''. As in the Fuchsian case, arithmetic Kleinian groups are discrete subgroups of finite covolume.

== Trace fields of arithmetic Fuchsian groups ==

The invariant [[trace field]] of a Fuchsian group (or, through the [[monodromy]] image of the fundamental group, of a hyperbolic surface) is the field generated by the traces of the squares of its elements. In the case of an arithmetic surface whose [[fundamental group]] is commensurable with a Fuchsian group derived from a quaternion algebra over a number field <math>F</math>, the invariant trace field equals <math>F</math>.

One can characterise arithmetic manifolds through the traces of the elements of their fundamental group, a result known as Takeuchi's criterion.{{sfn|Katok|1992|loc=Chapter 5}} A Fuchsian group is an arithmetic group if and only if the following three conditions are realised:
*Its invariant trace field <math>F</math> is a totally real number field; 
*The traces of its elements are [[algebraic integer]]s; 
*There is an embedding <math>\sigma: F \to \R</math> such that for any <math>\gamma</math> in the group, <math>t=\mathrm{Trace}(\gamma^2)</math> and for any other embedding <math>\sigma \neq \sigma': F \to \R</math> we have <math>|\sigma'(t)| \leqslant 2</math>.

== Geometry of arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces ==

The Lie group <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\R)</math> is the group of positive [[Isometry|isometries]] of the hyperbolic plane <math>\mathbb H^2</math>. Thus, if <math> \Gamma</math> is a discrete subgroup of <math>\mathrm{PSL}_2(\R)</math>, then <math>\Gamma</math> acts [[Properly discontinuous action|properly discontinuously]] on <math>\mathbb H^2</math>. If moreover <math>\Gamma</math> is [[Torsion (algebra)|torsion-free]], then the action is [[Group action (mathematics)#free|free]] and the quotient space <math>\Gamma \setminus \mathbb H^2</math> is a [[Surface (mathematics)|surface]] (a 2-manifold) with a [[hyperbolic manifold|hyperbolic metric]] (a [[Riemannian metric]] of constant sectional curvature −1). If <math>\Gamma</math> is an arithmetic Fuchsian group, then such a surface <math>S</math> is called an ''arithmetic hyperbolic surface'' (not to be confused with the [[arithmetic surface]]s from [[arithmetic geometry]]; however, when the context is clear the "hyperbolic" specifier may be omitted). Since arithmetic Fuchsian groups are of finite covolume, arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces always have finite Riemannian volume (i.e. the integral over <math>S</math> of the [[Volume form#Riemannian volume form|volume form]] is finite).

=== Volume formula and finiteness ===

It is possible to give a formula for the volume of distinguished arithmetic surfaces from the arithmetic data with which it was constructed. Let <math>\mathcal O</math> be a maximal order in the quaternion algebra <math>A</math> of [[Quaternion algebra#Quaternion algebras over the rational numbers|discriminant]] <math>D_A</math> over the field <math>F</math>, let <math>r = [F : \Q]</math> be its degree, <math>D_F</math> its [[Discriminant of a number field|discriminant]], and <math>\zeta_F</math> its [[Dedekind zeta function]]. Let <math>\Gamma_{\mathcal O}</math> be the arithmetic group obtained from <math>\mathcal O</math> by the procedure above and <math>S</math> the [[orbifold]] <math>\Gamma_{\mathcal O} \setminus \mathbb H^2</math>. Its volume is computed by the formula<ref>{{cite journal | last= Borel | first=Armand |title=Commensurability classes and volumes of hyperbolic 3-manifolds| journal=Ann. Scuola Norm. Sup.Pisa Cl. Sci.| volume= 8 | year=1981| pages=1–33}}</ref>

: <math> \operatorname{vol}(S) =  \frac {2 |D_F|^{\frac 3 2} \cdot \zeta_F(2)} {(2\pi)^{2r - 2}} \cdot \prod_{\mathfrak p \mid D_A} (N(\mathfrak p) - 1).</math>

The product is taken over [[prime ideal]]s of <math>O_F</math> dividing <math>(D_A)</math>, and <math>N(\cdot)</math> is the [[Field norm#Further properties|norm]] function on ideals, i.e. <math>N(\mathfrak p)</math> is the cardinality of the finite ring <math>O_F /\mathfrak p</math>. If <math>\mathcal O = M_2(\Z)</math>, then the output of this formula recovers the well-known result that the hyperbolic volume of the modular surface equals <math>\pi/3</math>.

Coupled with the description of maximal subgroups and finiteness results for number fields, this formula allows one to prove the following statement:

:''Given any <math>V > 0</math>, there are only finitely many arithmetic surfaces whose volume is less than <math>V</math>.''

Note that in dimensions ≥ 4, [[Wang's finiteness theorem]] (a consequence of [[local rigidity]]) asserts that this statement remains true by replacing "arithmetic" by "finite volume". An asymptotic equivalent for the number of arithmetic manifolds of a certain volume was given by Belolipetsky–[[Tsachik Gelander|Gelander]][[Alexander Lubotzky|–Lubotzky–]][[Shahar Mozes|Mozes]].<ref>{{cite journal| last1=Belolipetsky |first1=Misha |last2=Gelander |first2=Tsachik| last3=Lubotzky| first3=Alexander |last4=Shalev| first4=Aner |title=Counting arithmetic lattices and surfaces| journal=Ann. of Math. | year=2010|volume=172 |issue=3 |pages=2197–2221 | doi=10.4007/annals.2010.172.2197|arxiv=0811.2482}}</ref>

=== Minimal volume ===
{{Main article | Hurwitz surface}}

The hyperbolic orbifold of minimal volume can be obtained as the surface associated to a particular order, the [[Hurwitz quaternion order]], and it is compact of volume <math>\pi/21</math>.

=== Closed geodesics and injectivity radii ===

A [[closed geodesic]] on a [[Riemannian manifold]] is a [[closed curve]] that is also [[geodesic]]. One can give an effective description of the set of such curves in an arithmetic surface or 3-manifold: they correspond to certain units in certain quadratic extensions of the base field (the description is lengthy and shall not be given in full here). For example, the length of primitive closed geodesics in the modular surface corresponds to the absolute value of units of norm one in real quadratic fields. This description was used by [[Peter Sarnak|Sarnak]] to establish a conjecture of [[Carl Friedrich Gauss|Gauss]] on the mean order of [[class group]]s of real quadratic fields.<ref>{{cite journal| last=Sarnak| first= Peter| title= Class numbers of indefinite binary quadratic forms| journal= J. Number Theory| volume=15 | issue= 2|year=1982| pages= 229–247 | doi=10.1016/0022-314x(82)90028-2| doi-access= free}}</ref>

Arithmetic surfaces can be used<ref>{{cite journal |last=Katz |first=M. |last2=Schaps |first2=M. |last3=Vishne |first3=U. |title= Logarithmic growth of systole of arithmetic Riemann surfaces along congruence subgroups |journal=J. Differential Geom. |volume=76 |year=2007 |issue=3 |pages= 399–422 |arxiv= math.DG/0505007 |doi=10.4310/jdg/1180135693}}</ref> to construct families of surfaces of genus <math>g</math> for any <math>g</math> which satisfy the (optimal, up to a constant) [[Systoles of surfaces|systolic inequality]]

: <math> \operatorname{sys}(S) \geqslant \frac{4}{3} \log g.</math>

== Spectra of arithmetic hyperbolic surfaces ==

=== Laplace eigenvalues and eigenfunctions ===
{{Main article | Spectral geometry}}

If <math>S</math> is a hyperbolic surface, then there is a distinguished operator <math>\Delta</math> on [[smooth function]]s on <math>S</math>. In the case where <math>S</math> is compact it extends to an [[Unbounded operator|unbounded]], [[Unbounded operator#Extensions of symmetric operators|essentially self-adjoint]] operator on the [[Hilbert space]] <math>L^2(S)</math> of [[square-integrable function]]s on <math>S</math>. The spectral theorem in Riemannian geometry states that there exists an [[Hilbert space#orthonormal basis|orthonormal basis]] <math>\phi_0, \phi_1, \ldots, \phi_n, \ldots</math> of [[eigenfunction]]s for <math>\Delta</math>. The associated [[eigenvalue]]s <math>\lambda_0 = 0 < \lambda_1 \leqslant \lambda_2 \leqslant \cdots</math> are unbounded and their asymptotic behaviour is ruled by [[Weyl's law]].

In the case where <math>S = \Gamma \setminus \mathbb H^2</math> is arithmetic, these eigenfunctions are a special type of [[automorphic form]]s for <math>\Gamma</math> called [[Maass form]]s. The eigenvalues of <math>\Delta</math> are of interest for number theorists, as well as the distribution and [[???|nodal set]]s of the <math>\phi_n</math>.

The case where <math>S</math> is of finite volume is more complicated, but a similar theory can be established via the notion of [[cusp form]].

=== Selberg conjecture ===
{{Main article | Selberg's 1/4 conjecture}}

The ''spectral gap'' of the surface <math>S</math> is by definition the gap between the smallest eigenvalue <math>\lambda_0 = 0</math> and the second smallest eigenvalue <math>\lambda_1 > 0</math>; thus its value equals <math>\lambda_1</math>, and we shall denote it by <math>\lambda_1(S).</math> In general it can be made arbitrarily small (ref Randol) (however, it has a positive lower bound for a surface with fixed volume). The Selberg conjecture is the following statement providing a conjectural uniform lower bound in the arithmetic case:

:''If <math>\Gamma \subset \mathrm{PSL}_2(\R)</math> is a lattice which is derived from a quaternion algebra and <math>\Gamma'</math> is a torsion-free congruence subgroup of <math>\Gamma,</math> then for <math>S = \Gamma' \setminus \mathbb H^2</math> we have'' <math>\lambda_1(S) \geqslant \tfrac{1}{4}.</math>

The statement is only valid for a subclass of arithmetic surfaces and can be seen to be false for general subgroups of finite index in lattices derived from quaternion algebras. Selberg's original statement<ref>{{Citation | last1=Selberg | first1=Atle | editor1-last=Whiteman | editor1-first=Albert Leon | title=Theory of Numbers | chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6xAZAQAAIAAJ | publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] | location=Providence, R.I. | series=Proceedings of Symposia in Pure Mathematics | isbn=978-0-8218-1408-6  | mr=0182610 | year=1965 | volume=VIII | chapter=On the estimation of Fourier coefficients of modular forms | pages=1–15}}</ref> was made only for congruence covers of the modular surface, and it has been verified for some small groups.<ref>{{cite journal| last= Roelcke |first=W. | title=Über die Wellengleichung bei Grenzkreisgruppen erster Art| journal=S.-B. Heidelberger Akad. Wiss. Math.-Nat. Kl. 1953/1955 |pages= 159–267 | language=german}}</ref> Selberg himself proved the lower bound <math>\lambda_1 \geqslant \tfrac{1}{16},</math> a result known as Selberg's 1/16 theorem. The best known result in full generality is due to Luo–Rudnick–Sarnak.<ref>{{cite journal| last1 = Kim | first1=H. H. | title=Functoriality for the exterior square of <math>GL_4</math> and the symmetric fourth of <math>GL_2</math> | others = With appendix 1 by Dinakar Ramakrishnan and appendix 2 by Kim and Peter Sarnak |journal= J. Amer. Math. Soc. |volume = 16 | year = 2003 | pages=139–183| doi=10.1090/S0894-0347-02-00410-1 | doi-access= free }}</ref>

The uniformity of the spectral gap has implications for the construction of [[expander graph]]s as Schreier graphs of <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\Z).</math><ref>{{cite book |last=Lubotzky |first=Alexander |title=Discrete groups, expanding graphs and invariant measures |publisher=Birkhäuser | date=1994}}</ref>

=== Relations with geometry ===
{{Main article | Selberg's trace formula }}
{{Main article | Cheeger constant}}

Selberg's trace formula shows that, for a hyperbolic surface of finite volume, it is equivalent to know the length spectrum (the collection of lengths of all closed geodesics on <math>S</math>, with multiplicities) and the spectrum of <math>\Delta</math>. However, the precise relation is not explicit.

Another relation between spectrum and geometry is given by [[Cheeger constant#Cheeger's inequality|Cheeger's inequality]], which in the case of a surface <math>S</math> states roughly that a positive lower bound on the spectral gap of <math>S</math> translates into a positive lower bound for the total length of a collection of smooth closed curves separating <math>S</math> into two connected components.

=== Quantum ergodicity ===
{{Main article | Quantum ergodicity }}

The [[quantum ergodicity]] theorem of Alexander Shnirelmann, [[Yves Colin de Verdière]], and [[Steven Zelditch]] states that on average, eigenfunctions equidistribute on <math>S</math>. The unique quantum ergodicity conjecture of [[Zeev Rudnick]] and [[Peter Sarnak]] asks whether the stronger statement that individual eigenfunctions equidistribute is true. Formally, the statement is as follows.

:''Let  <math>S</math> be an arithmetic surface and <math>\phi_j</math> be a sequence of functions on <math>S</math> such that'' 
::<math>\Delta\phi_j = \lambda_j\phi_j, \qquad \int_S \phi_j(x)^2 \,dx = 1.</math>
:''Then for any smooth, compactly supported function <math>\psi</math> on <math>S</math> we have''
::<math> \lim_{j\to \infty} \left( \int_S \psi(x) \phi_j(x)^2 \,dx \right) = \int_S \psi(x)\,dx.</math>

This conjecture was proved by [[Elon Lindenstrauss]]<ref>{{ cite journal |last= Lindenstrauss | first=Elon |title=Invariant measures and arithmetic quantum unique ergodicity |journal= Ann. of Math.| volume=163 | date=2006 | pages=165–219 | doi=10.4007/annals.2006.163.165| doi-access=free }}</ref> in the case where <math>S</math> is compact and the <math>\phi_j</math> are additionally eigenfunctions for the [[Hecke operator]]s on <math>S</math>. In the case of congruence covers of the modular some additional difficulties occur, which were dealt with by [[Kannan Soundararajan]].<ref>{{cite journal | last= Soundararajan | first=Kannan |title=Quantum unique ergodicity for <math>\mathrm{SL}_2(\Z) \setminus \mathcal H</math>| journal=Ann. of Math. | volume=172 |date=2010 |pages= 1529–1538 |doi=10.4007/annals.2010.172.1529 |mr= 2680500|url=http://annals.math.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/annals-v172-n2-p19-s.pdf|jstor=29764647}}</ref>

=== Isospectral surfaces ===
{{Main article | Isospectral}}

The fact that for arithmetic surfaces the arithmetic data determines the spectrum of the Laplace operator <math>\Delta</math> was pointed out by [[Marie-France Vignéras]]<ref>{{cite journal | last=Vignéras | first=Marie-France | title=Variétés riemanniennes isospectrales et non isométriques | language=French | journal=Ann. of Math. | volume=112 | issue=1 | date=1980 | pages=21–32 | doi=10.2307/1971319| jstor=1971319 }}</ref> and used by her to construct examples of isospectral compact hyperbolic surfaces. The precise statement is as follows:

:''If <math>A</math> is a quaternion algebra, <math>\mathcal O_1, \mathcal O_2</math> are maximal orders in <math>A</math>'', ''and the associated Fuchsian groups <math>\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2</math> are torsion-free, then the hyperbolic surfaces <math>S_i = \Gamma_i \setminus \mathbb H^2</math> have the same Laplace spectrum. ''

Vignéras then constructed explicit instances for <math>A, \mathcal O_1, \mathcal O_2</math> satisfying the conditions above and such that in addition <math>\mathcal O_2</math> is not conjugated by an element of <math>A</math> to <math>\mathcal O_1</math>. The resulting isospectral hyperbolic surfaces are then not isometric.
